problem: Learning-based social robot navigation has mostly used a single sensor modality, and there has been little systematic study of how combining LiDAR point clouds and RGB images affects socially compliant global and local decisions compared with unimodal learning and classical planners.
motivation: Socially compliant navigation needs geometric information (obstacles, humans) and semantic information (gaze, gesture, terrain, body language). LiDAR and RGB provide these respectively, so fusing them should help, especially in dense crowds. This paper checks that empirically on a large real-world dataset and with a human study.
key_idea: Train the same behavior-cloning architecture (global waypoint plan plus local velocity plan) on SCAND with LiDAR only, RGB only, or feature-fused multimodal input, and compare them against classical planners in offline tests and a human study.
insight: Multimodal fusion gives the lowest and fastest-converging test loss on all eight test SCAND rosbags. RGB-only degrades most as human density rises, with loss more than doubling in crowded, confined scenarios, while point cloud stays stable. Fusion beats point cloud alone, which the authors attribute to the extra semantic cues. In the human study, however, multimodal shows no significant advantage over point cloud, probably because the curated scenarios lack rich semantic cues.
method: Problem formulation: behavior cloning from SCAND. Input is LiDAR point cloud L, RGB image I and a goal 2.5 m ahead on future odometry, with history N=1. Output is a global plan of 5 waypoints (0.5 m apart, M=5) and a local plan of current (v, ω) (K=1).

Point cloud encoder: LiDAR points within 8 m ahead, 3 m to each side and 2.5 m height are voxelized at 5 cm into a 160x120x50 grid and encoded by a 3D CNN (VoxNet-style). PointNet and PointNet++ performed worse.

Decision modules: encoder embedding plus goal go to an RNN, then an MLP gives the global waypoints. Those waypoints go through another MLP, are concatenated with the RNN output, and pass through a transformer and an MLP to give the velocity commands. A plain MLP local planner failed to capture the variation.
Multimodal fusion: the RNN outputs of the point cloud and image branches are concatenated at two places, one for the global plan and one for the local plan.
Loss: L2 on the 5 waypoints plus L1 on the velocity commands, with λ=1. Training uses 18 SCAND trials and testing uses 8, averaged over 3 runs.

Human study: Jackal with VLP-16 and ZED2, 8 participants, frontal approach with 1 or 2 humans, 5-item questionnaire from Pirk et al. Multimodal is compared with move_base, the best classical planner by loss. The RGB-only policy was excluded because it moved dangerously close to people.

setting.backbone: 3D CNN (voxel LiDAR) + ResNet-18 (RGB) + RNN + transformer + MLPs, trained from scratch with behavior cloning
setting.training_data: SCAND (8.7 h, 138 trajectories, 40 km of human teleoperated socially compliant demonstrations on Spot and Jackal); 18 trials for training, 8 for testing
setting.observation: 3D LiDAR point cloud (voxelized) + monocular RGB 224x224, plus a local goal 2.5 m ahead
setting.action_space: global plan of 5 2D waypoints (0.5 m apart) and local plan of linear and angular velocity commands
setting.simulator: real world only (offline SCAND dataset and a physical Jackal human study)
setting.privileged: none (the goal waypoint is taken from future odometry in the dataset)

numbers_note: Results are given only as loss curves (Figs. 3-4) and human-study bar charts (Fig. 5), with no numeric tables and no standard navigation metrics.
results: Multimodal learning has lower test loss than both unimodal variants and the classical planners on the SCAND test rosbags for global planning, and slightly lower for local planning. The point cloud policy beats RGB. In the human study with the Jackal, multimodal scores higher and with lower variance than move_base on all 5 questions, and the gap grows with two humans. It is not clearly better than point cloud only.
limitations: Evaluation is offline on pre-recorded data plus small curated human-study scenarios (8 participants, outdoor frontal approach), not long-term real-world navigation.
The RGB-only policy was not tested in the human study for safety reasons, and history length is fixed at N=1.
No quantitative numeric tables are reported; the results are shown only in curves and charts.
builds_on: Pirk et al. social navigation protocol
